entry.title: Exploring Change Data Capture with Debezium and Jupyter

link.title: Exploring Change Data Capture with Debezium and Jupyter

entry.content:
When people think about Debezium integrations, the first idea is usually a production pipeline: capture changes from a database, deliver them to Kafka, and route them to downstream services or analytical systems. That is, of course, a very common and very good use case. But there is another side to change data capture that deserves attention too: exploration.

Sometimes you do not want to start with a full deployment and a chain of consumers. Sometimes you want to inspect the events, validate a connector configuration, build a quick proof of concept, or show colleagues what the stream actually looks like. In these situations, an interactive environment can be much more effective than a traditional application.

This is where Jupyter notebooks fit surprisingly well.

In this post, we will look at a simple Debezium and Jupyter integration based on the jupyter example in the debezium-examples repository. The demo runs Debezium Engine from a notebook by using pydbzengine, captures changes from PostgreSQL, stores the resulting records in a pandas data frame, and lets you inspect and aggregate them interactively.

Why Jupyter?

Jupyter is usually associated with data science, experimentation, and teaching. All three are relevant to CDC as well.

When working with Debezium, there are several recurring tasks for which notebooks can be very convenient:

  • exploring the structure of change events without writing a full consumer application,

  • validating connector properties and table filters,

  • demonstrating snapshots and streaming phases during workshops or internal training,

  • performing ad-hoc analysis over captured events with pandas,

  • troubleshooting whether changes are actually emitted for a particular table or primary key.

This does not mean that Jupyter replaces Kafka Connect, Debezium Server, or the embedded engine in a production deployment. It does not. What it gives you is a very low-friction working environment for understanding your data stream before you decide what should happen with it next.

The interesting part is that the integration is not based on any artificial mock. The notebook uses the same Debezium connector logic that you would use elsewhere. The only difference is the runtime environment and the consumer implementation.

The Example

The demo is intentionally small. It uses two containers:

  • a PostgreSQL instance based on the Debezium tutorial database,

  • a Jupyter Lab container with Python dependencies and a JDK installed.

The complete example is available in debezium-examples/jupyter.

The flow is straightforward:

  1. PostgreSQL stores the source data.

  2. Debezium Engine runs inside the notebook kernel through pydbzengine.

  3. A Python change handler receives Debezium events.

  4. The handler converts the incoming records into Python structures.

  5. pandas is used to inspect and aggregate the captured changes.

This is a good example of a pattern that is often overlooked. Debezium is not limited to "database to Kafka" pipelines. If you can consume change events in-process, you can place Debezium into developer tools, notebooks, scripts, and exploratory workflows too.

Starting the Demo

The example is designed to be easy to run locally. From the jupyter directory in debezium-examples, start it with:

docker compose up --build

Once the services are ready, open Jupyter Lab at http://localhost:8888. The prepared notebook is named postgres_cdc_pk_change_counts.ipynb.

The environment is configured via Docker Compose. The Jupyter container receives the PostgreSQL connection settings as well as several Debezium properties, for example:

environment:
  PG_HOST: postgres
  PG_PORT: "5432"
  PG_USER: postgres
  PG_PASSWORD: postgres
  PG_DBNAME: postgres
  TABLE_INCLUDE_LIST: inventory.customers
  SCHEMA_INCLUDE_LIST: inventory
  TOPIC_PREFIX: dbserver1
  SLOT_NAME: pydbzengine_slot
  PLUGIN_NAME: pgoutput
  SNAPSHOT_MODE: initial

This is already enough to show an important point. The notebook is not built around hardcoded sample logic only. You can adjust the target table, schema, replication slot, or snapshot behavior and immediately observe the effect. For workshops and experiments, that feedback loop is very useful.

Configuring Debezium in the Notebook

The notebook starts by defining the connector configuration in Python:

dbz_props = {
    'name': 'pydbzengine-postgres-to-pandas',
    'connector.class': 'io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector',
    'database.hostname': PG_HOST,
    'database.port': PG_PORT,
    'database.user': PG_USER,
    'database.password': PG_PASSWORD,
    'database.dbname': PG_DBNAME,
    'topic.prefix': TOPIC_PREFIX,
    'schema.include.list': SCHEMA_INCLUDE_LIST,
    'table.include.list': TABLE_INCLUDE_LIST,
    'slot.name': SLOT_NAME,
    'plugin.name': PLUGIN_NAME,
    'publication.autocreate.mode': PUBLICATION_AUTOCREATE_MODE,
    'include.schema.changes': 'false',
    'snapshot.mode': SNAPSHOT_MODE,
    'offset.storage': 'org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.FileOffsetBackingStore',
    'offset.storage.file.filename': OFFSET_FILE,
    'offset.flush.interval.ms': '1000'
}

If you have configured Debezium connectors before, this should look very familiar. That is precisely the benefit. The notebook approach does not introduce a new conceptual model. It reuses the same connector properties and the same source connector implementation.

In other words, the distance between "I am experimenting in a notebook" and "I am configuring a real Debezium deployment" stays small. That reduces surprises later.

The example uses PostgreSQL and captures changes from inventory.customers. For a first notebook-based CDC demo this is a sensible choice, because the table is small, easy to understand, and already known from the tutorial.

Collecting Records in Python

The core of the integration is a very small Python change handler. It receives records from Debezium and stores a normalized representation in memory:

class DataFrameCollector(BasePythonChangeHandler):
    def handleJsonBatch(self, records: List[ChangeEvent]):
        rows = []
        for record in records:
            key_raw = _as_python_str(record.key())
            key_json = json.loads(key_raw if key_raw else '{}')
            value_raw = _as_python_str(record.value())

            value_json = json.loads(value_raw)
            payload = value_json.get('payload', {})

            rows.append({
                'destination': _as_python_str(record.destination()),
                'pk': json.dumps(key_json, sort_keys = True),
                'op': payload.get('op'),
                'ts_ms': payload.get('ts_ms'),
                'before': payload.get('before'),
                'after': payload.get('after'),
            })

This is probably my favorite part of the demo because it shows how little code is needed to become productive.

The handler does not try to solve every possible processing scenario. It simply extracts a few useful fields:

  • destination,

  • primary key,

  • operation type,

  • event timestamp,

  • before state,

  • after state.

That is enough to inspect snapshots, updates, and deletes, and to build compact summaries on top of them.

The notebook then turns the in-memory list into a pandas data frame. From there you can use standard Python data analysis techniques instead of writing custom Java or Kafka consumer logic.

For example, a timestamp column is derived from ts_ms, making it easy to sort, filter, or plot events later.

Running the Engine Interactively

Debezium Engine is a blocking process, so the notebook starts it in a background thread. Again, the implementation is intentionally minimal:

def start_engine():
    global engine, engine_thread
    engine = DebeziumJsonEngine(properties = dbz_props, handler = DataFrameCollector())
    engine_thread = threading.Thread(target = engine.run, daemon = True)
    engine_thread.start()
    print('Engine started in background.')

def stop_engine():
    global engine, engine_thread
    engine.close()
    if engine_thread is not None:
        engine_thread.join(timeout = 10)
    print('Engine stopped.')

This is one of the areas where Jupyter provides a noticeably better experience than a standalone command-line example. You can start the engine, leave it running, execute SQL changes, inspect captured events, run another batch of SQL statements, and continue analysis in the same session.

The demo adds ipywidgets buttons on top of these functions:

  • Start Engine

  • Run Sample SQL

  • Stop Engine

That makes the notebook suitable not only for developers, but also for demos and technical presentations. Instead of switching among several terminals, you keep the setup, execution, and analysis in a single view.

Generating and Inspecting Changes

To produce a stream of updates, the notebook contains a helper function that modifies records in the source table:

def run_sample_changes(pk: int = SAMPLE_PK):
    sql_statements = [
        'SET search_path TO inventory',
        f'UPDATE customers SET first_name = first_name || \'-x\' WHERE id = {pk}'
    ]

This is intentionally simple, but very effective for demonstration purposes. After you start the engine and execute the sample SQL, you can refresh the data frame cell and immediately see additional change events.

The notebook also makes the distinction between snapshot and streaming events visible. Debezium operation codes are preserved, so you can decide whether snapshot reads (r) should be counted together with actual changes (c, u, d) or filtered out.

That is something many people struggle with when they first start consuming Debezium events. Seeing it in a notebook helps a lot.

For example, the aggregation cell counts changes per primary key:

ops = ['c', 'u', 'd']
working_df = records_dataframe()

change_counts = (
    working_df[working_df['op'].fillna('').astype(str).isin(ops)]
    .groupby('pk', as_index = False)
    .size()
    .rename(columns = {'size': 'change_count'})
    .sort_values('change_count', ascending = False)
)

This is exactly the kind of analysis that would be cumbersome if you only inspected raw JSON in logs. With pandas, it becomes trivial.

And once the data is in a data frame, you can naturally extend the notebook further:

  • compare activity across keys,

  • inspect change velocity over time,

  • identify hot rows,

  • validate whether a filter includes the expected tables,

  • experiment with delete handling and snapshots.

Why This Matters

At the first glance, a notebook may seem like a toy compared to a full CDC pipeline. I do not think that is the right way to look at it.

Interactive environments are often the fastest route to clarity. When a team evaluates CDC for a new use case, the first obstacle is usually not throughput or deployment topology. It is understanding the shape and semantics of the emitted events.

Questions tend to be very basic:

  • What does the key look like?

  • What is in before and after?

  • How do snapshot records differ from streaming updates?

  • Did my table filter work?

  • Are deletes represented the way my downstream processing expects?

You can answer all these questions in a notebook in minutes.

There is also a broader Python angle here. A lot of analytical and data engineering work today happens in Python-first environments. By using pydbzengine, Debezium becomes accessible in that ecosystem without forcing users to abandon the tools they already know.

This does not replace the Java APIs, Kafka-based deployments, or Debezium Server. It complements them. In practice, that means:

  • analysts can explore CDC interactively,

  • data engineers can prototype consumers quickly,

  • platform teams can validate source behavior before provisioning infrastructure,

  • educators can explain Debezium concepts with immediate feedback.

Where to Go Next

The provided demo intentionally keeps the scope narrow. It focuses on one table, one notebook, and one simple aggregation. That is the right choice for a first example, but it should also give you ideas for extensions.

For instance, you could:

  • capture multiple tables and analyze them together

  • flatten events before analysis

  • persist the captured records into Parquet or DuckDB

  • visualize event rates with matplotlib

  • connect the notebook to a machine learning workflow

  • compare snapshot and streaming latency under different connector settings

If this sounds familiar, it should. We already saw in earlier Debezium examples that notebooks can be useful for machine learning scenarios too. The difference here is that the new Jupyter example is much more direct: it focuses on CDC exploration itself instead of using the notebook only as a UI on top of another pipeline.

That makes it a good building block for many other demos.

Final Thoughts

Debezium is often introduced through large-scale streaming architectures, and rightly so. But one of its strengths is that the same CDC foundation can be applied at very different scales and in very different runtimes.

The Jupyter integration shows that Debezium can be just as useful in an interactive notebook as it is in a production data pipeline. You can configure a real connector, capture real change events, and analyze them with familiar Python tools in a matter of minutes.

If you are evaluating Debezium, teaching CDC concepts, or simply trying to understand the behavior of a source table, this is a very practical place to start. And if you already use Debezium in production, a notebook like this can become a handy addition to your toolbox for experimentation, validation, and troubleshooting.

You can find the full demo in the debezium-examples repository. If you build on top of it, let us know what kind of notebook-based CDC workflows you find useful.
entry.summary: When people think about Debezium integrations, the first idea is usually a production pipeline: capture changes from a database, deliver them to Kafka, and route them to downstream services or analytical systems. That is, of course, a very common and very good use case. But there is another side to change data capture that deserves attention too: exploration. Sometimes you do not want to start with a full deployment and a chain of consumers. Sometimes you want to inspect the events, validate a connector configuration, build a quick proof of concept, or show colleagues what the stream actually looks like. In these situations, an interactive environment can be much more effective than a traditional application. This is where Jupyter notebooks fit surprisingly well. In this post, we will look at a simple Debezium and Jupyter integration based on the jupyter example in the debezium-examples repository. The demo runs Debezium Engine from a notebook by using pydbzengine, captures changes from PostgreSQL, stores the resulting records in a pandas data frame, and lets you inspect and aggregate them interactively.

entry.title: What the Debezium Community Told Us - 2026 Survey Results

link.title: What the Debezium Community Told Us - 2026 Survey Results

entry.content:
Earlier this year, we asked the Debezium community to tell us how they’re using the project, what’s working, and where we need to do better. We received numerous responses, and we appreciate the candid, detailed, and genuinely useful information that people took the time to share.

This post is going to walk you through all the key findings. We’re sharing everything with the public, which will include not only the things that we’re proud of or that surprised us, but equally important the things we need to fix.

Who Responded

The Debezium community is more diverse than you might expect. Respondents came from over 30 industries: Software and SaaS, FinTech, Healthcare, Gaming, Logistics, Retail, Manufacturing, Media, Government, Insurance, IoT, Gambling, Fashion, Telecommunications, and even Water and Waste Utility services. It turns out, Change Data Capture (CDC) is clearly a universal need.

The majority of the respondents, 60.9%, work at organizations with more than 500 employees, which tells us Debezium is firmly established in enterprise environments. But smaller teams are well represented too, with 10.1% coming from organizations of 11-50 people, and 7.2% from teams of 10 or fewer.

Across these organizations, roles ranged from architects and engineers to directors, VPs, and management information system (MIS) specialists. The people operating Debezium in production sit across the entire technical org chart.

The Numbers We’re Most Proud Of

Let’s start with the headline: 65.2% of respondents gave Debezium a 5 out of 5 when asked how likely they are to recommend it. Another 20.3% gave it a 4. Only 1.4% rated it a 2, and no one rated it a 1.

This is a strong signal the community is clearly using Debezium in serious, mission-critical production deployments.

Additionally, Debezium’s adoption numbers tell a compelling story: nearly all respondents (98.6%), are either actively using it or plan to within the next year, with 91.3% of those already in active use today. With only 4.3% of respondents having moved to a competing solution or no longer needing a CDC at all, the retention speaks for itself.

What "Production Debezium" Actually Looks Like

The scale at which people are running Debezium is worth pausing on.

How many changes per minute does your system experience?

When we asked about change throughput, responses ranged from as low as 1-25 changes per minute up to 1-2 million changes per minute. Many environments operate in the tens or hundreds of thousands per minute.

While survey respondents reported throughput ranging from thousands to millions of changes per minute, these numbers reflect only a snapshot of the broader Debezium community.

Debezium is deployed in production environments processing hundreds of thousands of events per second, demonstrating it scales well beyond what the survey captured.

On the deployment side, 63.8% run Debezium on Kubernetes and 60.9% use self-managed Kafka Connect.

Helm charts are the dominant configuration management approach, often combined with GitOps, CI/CD pipelines, Ansible, or Terraform. Strimzi is widely used. A smaller but meaningful segment (17.4%) still run Debezium on virtual machines or bare metal.

The connector picture is led by PostgreSQL at 69.6%, followed by MySQL (33.3%), SQL Server (29%), JDBC sink (29%), and Oracle (27.5%). MongoDB has remarkable representation alongside its relational counterparts at 20.3%.

Which connectors do you use?

Beyond connectors, 91.3% use Debezium’s connectors as their primary component, with Debezium Server (26.1%) and the Embedded Engine (11.6%) seeing meaningful adoption.

Use cases span the full range of what CDC enables: real-time applications, auditing, data warehousing, CQRS patterns, AI data ingestion, payment processing, multi-database consolidation into Databricks, and more.

The Skills Debezium Requires

Operating Debezium well requires a genuine breadth of expertise. Respondents identified five key skill areas:

Database internals and administration

Understanding replication mechanisms used by the source database, often times at a low level.

Kafka and data streaming

Familiarity with Kafka, Kafka Connect, and the broader streaming ecosystem.

Operational and DevOps

Kubernetes, Docker, Helm, Terraform

Architectural and system design

Designing end-to-end data flows, managing integrations, and reasoning about distributed systems.

Programming and configuration

Java is needed if you need to create any custom converters, transforms, or implement custom connectors. It’s also critical if you need to do any sort of memory debugging due to out of memory concerns.

In total, 79.7% of the respondents said their team has the skills to operate Debezium. That means 1 in 5 respondents don’t believe their team has the skills. That’s a meaningful gap, and it has real implications for what we need to improve on in terms of documentation, tooling, and the overall user experience.

Where Debezium Falls Short

When we asked what’s difficult to use, what’s missing, and what the website lacks, the responses clustered into clear themes.

Documentation Gaps

The overall assessment of Debezium’s documentation was positive, respondents recognized it as thorough. But "thorough" and "complete" are vastly different things. What’s missing, according to the community:

  • Deep-drive guides for managed services: there is a clear desire for in-depth guides that outline environment-specific setups for cloud providers.

  • Operational and troubleshooting content: monitoring, debugging, management commands, and best practices are hard to find or absent.

  • Better Search: the website search experience needs significant improvement

  • End-to-end examples: while Debezium does provide a wide array of examples, the community is looking for complex, realistic demos covering multi-connector setups and production-grade configurations.

Management and Observability

The single most consistent request was for a Web UI or console portal for managing Debezium deployments. When asked which runtimes they’d manage via a Web UI, respondents said Kafka Connect (75.4%), Debezium Server (40.6%), and Kubernetes/OpenShift using Debezium Platform (34.8%).

Which runtimes would you manage via a web UI?

Kafka Connect75.4%
Debezium Server40.6%
Kubernetes / OpenShift34.8%
3 in 4 respondents want a web UI for managing Kafka Connect
Survey respondents could select all deployment targets that apply. Percentages reflect the share of respondents using each option and may sum to more than 100%.

Configuration complexity, debugging difficulty, and lack of observability came up repeatedly. Respondents want better visibility into what Debezium is doing, and easier ways to manage it when things go wrong.

Missing capabilities

Specific gaps that multiple respondents highlighted include:

  • Automatic incremental snapshots for newly added tables, or the ability to do partial snapshots.

  • DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) improvement for sink connectors including auto-reprocessing and better handling of missed events.

  • Graceful failover support

  • Schema history cleanup and compaction

  • Better support for combining or querying records from other tables during transformations

  • Time-series and ML/vector database integrations, more on this below

Connector Requests: Time-Series and Vector Are Next

When we asked what additional database connectors people want to see, time-series databases led at 34.8% and vector databases came in closely behind it at 31.9%.

What additional connectors would you like to see?

34.8%
Time-series databases
31.9%
Vector databases
Also requested: Graph (1.4%) · Snowflake sink (1.4%) · ElasticSearch (1.4%) · TiDB (1.4%) · 7.2% said no additional connectors needed

These aren’t niche requests, they reflect where data infrastructure is heading. AI and ML workloads need fresh, streaming data, and the community is clearly thinking about how Debezium fits into that picture.

The Contributor Community Has Room To Grow

Our respondents indicated that 23.2% of them have contributed to Debezium in the past, a meaningful base for an open-source project, but also a clear signal that most users haven’t made the jump from consumer to contributor. Of those who have contributed, 75% did not find the experience challenging, which suggests the barrier isn’t the contributing process itself necessarily.

For the 25% who did find the contributing experience challenging, the main friction points were environment and setup, code familiarity, and integration tests. These are the most common concerns when first contributing to a new code base. If we can find ways to help close those gaps and make it easier for the other 76.8% to find a way in, there’s a real opportunity to grow our contributor base.

How People Find Debezium

The majority of respondents found Debezium through our website (46.4%) or using search engines (17%). Social media accounted for approximately 16% while technical conferences accounted for 13%.

The dominance of organic search and direct website traffic tells us that Debezium’s reputation does the heavy lifting. People find it because they’re looking for a solution and it’s surfaces well on searches, and not because of any marketing campaigns.

What We’re Doing About It

The community feedback is extremely valuable to the project team. Acting on it is what matters, and here’s where the survey results are directly influencing our priorities:

Documentation

We are actively discussing how we can improve our overall website, including the documentation. This includes providing better troubleshooting and operational guides, managed service setup guides, and improved examples. We’ve also heard the feedback about better search, and we are actively exploring options. We are also integrating documentation directly into the Debezium Platform, providing a better in-context experience.

Management tooling

The demand for a web-based user interface is clear and consistent. The Debezium Platform is our answer to this, and the survey results reinforce that we need to continue investing in it. Monitoring and observability, along with guided workflows, are being integrated into the Platform.

Looking further ahead, notifications for incremental snapshots and Kubernetes event dispatching from the Debezium operator are already planned. We’re also exploring CLI-based tooling and host-based deployment options for Debezium Server; nothing to announce just yet, but it’s actively being explored, and we hope to have more soon.

Connector coverage

Time-series and vector databases are clearly on the community’s mind, and they’re on ours too. Debezium Server source connectors for Milvus and Qdrant are on the roadmap. A new graph database source connector, a SQLite source connector, and an Elasticsearch sink connector are all planned for later this year.

Operational improvements

Incremental snapshots and observability are both active areas. Micrometer monitoring via OpenTelemetry is on the roadmap. Multithreaded single table snapshots were introduced earlier this year to provide scalability for initial and blocking snapshots. Read-only incremental snapshots for SQL Server and Oracle are planned for a future release. Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) handling improvements are also on our radar.

Thank You

To everyone who took the time to fill out the survey, we want to thank you. The candor and detail in your responses, especially around what’s hard and what’s missing, is exactly what we need to continue to improve Debezium in ways that help you focus on what’s most important.

Debezium is what it is because of its vibrant and open community. Together, let’s keep building for tomorrow!

Have thoughts on the results or something we missed? Join the conversation on Debezium Zulip Chat.

entry.title: Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha1 Released

link.title: Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha1 Released

entry.content:
With spring in full swing, we’re kicking off the Debezium 3.6 cycle with 3.6.0.Alpha1, a preview release packed with improvements across the entire ecosystem.

Highlights include a new Docling transformation that enriches change events with structured document output directly in the pipeline, making it a natural fit for AI and retrieval-augmented generation workflows, and a brand-new Amazon SNS sink for Debezium Server that lets CDC events fan out to AWS messaging subscribers without an intermediate broker. Oracle users will also find a reworked LogMiner batch-sizing algorithm that trades hard-to-tune properties for a simpler, more predictable log file–based approach.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha1

Debezium for MongoDB

The MongoDB ExtractNewDocumentState SMT previously failed with an Avro SchemaParseException when collection names started with a digit (for example, 10019_AutoState), because the generated dotted schema name was validated segment-by-segment by Avro while Debezium’s name adjuster only inspected the overall string.

The SMT now derives a schema-level SchemaNameAdjuster from the field.name.adjustment.mode setting, splits the generated schema name on dots, and sanitizes each segment independently so that invalid leading characters are corrected (e.g., 10019_AutoState becomes _10019_AutoState). Because this adjustment only takes effect when field.name.adjustment.mode is set to avro or avro_unicode, users relying on Avro serialization with MongoDB collections whose names contain segments that are not valid Avro identifiers should be aware that emitted schema names will now be altered to conform to Avro rules.

Downstream consumers and schema registry entries may need to be updated accordingly before upgrading (dbz#305).

Debezium for PostgreSQL

The PostgreSQL connector now returns enum values in their logical PostgreSQL sort order rather than their internal storage order, ensuring that the allowed values list in the emitted schema metadata is stable and predictable across connectors and restarts.

Previously, two connectors capturing the same enum type could produce different value orderings, causing Avro schema mismatches for downstream consumers sharing a topic. Because the order of enum values in emitted schemas may change after upgrading, users relying on a specific ordering in their schema registry or downstream consumers should review and, if necessary, reconcile their schemas before upgrading (dbz#1331).

Note that when new values are inserted between existing enum values in PostgreSQL, the resulting allowed values list will reflect that logical position rather than appending to the end.

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MariaDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Debezium Operator

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium for Cassandra

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Informix

Container Images

Debezium Examples

Debezium Core

Tracking skipped, unchanged events

This release introduces a new streaming metric, NumberOfUnchangedEventsSkipped, that tracks how many events were skipped as a result of setting skip.messages.without.change to true.

Previously, operators had no way to observe the effect of this configuration, making it difficult to reason about filtering behavior or validate expected throughput reductions. The metric is exposed consistently across all connectors that support the skip.messages.without.change option (dbz#1026).

Docling Transformation

Debezium includes a new single message transformation (SMT) that integrates Docling, allowing selected text fields in change events to be converted into a unified document representation format.

By leveraging Docling’s document processing capabilities within the Debezium pipeline, users can normalize and enrich textual content as it streams from source databases to downstream systems. This is particularly useful for AI and data integration workflows where consistent, structured document output is required for downstream processing such as indexing, embedding generation, or retrieval-augmented generation (dbz#1442).

Transformation nested field improvements

Single Message Transforms that project values into nested fields of the record payload can now create intermediate structures on the fly when they don’t already exist. Previously, configuring an SMT such as HeaderToValue to write into a path like from_header.some_header would fail if the parent field from_header was not present in the payload, forcing users to ensure the target structure existed beforehand (dbz#1702).

With this enhancement, the common schema-construction utility shared across SMTs transparently materializes missing parent structs, making nested field targeting work out of the box. This removes a common source of configuration friction for users routing header values or other data into structured payload locations.

Configurable heartbeat.topic.name

Debezium connectors now support a new optional topic.heartbeat.name configuration property that lets users specify the exact heartbeat topic name, overriding the default {topic.heartbeat.prefix}.{topic.prefix} naming pattern. This is particularly useful in deployments running large numbers of source connectors, where each connector would otherwise create its own single-partition heartbeat topic, leading to unnecessary topic sprawl in Kafka.

By setting an explicit name, heartbeat events from multiple connectors can be consolidated into a single shared topic without resorting to custom TopicNamingStrategy implementations or RegexRouter transformations. The change is fully backward-compatible: if the property is left unset, connectors continue to use the existing prefix-based naming behavior (dbz#1709).

Improved transformation validation

Invalid enum values in Single Message Transform (SMT) configurations are now rejected at connector creation time rather than silently accepted and surfacing only later when the task attempts to start (dbz#1382). Previously, supplying an invalid value such as transforms.custom_unwrap.delete.handling.mode=abcd would allow the connector to be created successfully, with the failure only appearing once the task began running.

To address this, Debezium’s EnumRecommender now implements Kafka’s ConfigDef.Validator interface and Debezium validators are properly passed through to Kafka Connect’s ConfigDef, ensuring enum constraints are enforced during the standard configuration validation phase. This leads to faster feedback for users and avoids misleading "successful" connector creations that would otherwise fail at runtime.

Debezium for MariaDB

Adjust offset position using signals

The MariaDB connector now supports signal-based binlog position adjustment, bringing it on par with the equivalent MySQL capability introduced in DBZ-3829 (dbz#1755). Operators can send a signal to the connector to reposition it to a specific binlog file and offset, or to a particular GTID, allowing events to be re-read from a chosen point in the binlog.

This is particularly useful for recovery scenarios, reprocessing historical changes, or correcting pipelines after downstream issues, without having to resort to manual offset manipulation.

Debezium for MySQL

Ignore GTIDs for graceful recovery

The MySQL connector (and MariaDB) now supports a new gtid.ignore.on.recovery configuration option that allows the connector to fall back to binlog file/position when GTID-based recovery would otherwise fail (dbz#1385). This addresses a common operational pain point where purged or stale GTIDs on the server prevented the connector from resuming, forcing operators to manually reset the stored GTID offset.

When enabled, the flag only affects startup: GTID validation and positioning are skipped, the stale GTID is cleared from the offset, and the connector resumes from the stored binlog coordinates. Normal GTID tracking resumes once streaming starts again, so subsequent restarts can rely on fresh GTID state without any further intervention.

Debezium for Oracle

LogMiner mining algorithm performance improved

The Oracle connector’s LogMiner batch sizing has been reworked to address long-standing tuning difficulties, particularly in environments with bursty workloads or high-volume activity where the connector could struggle to catch up to near real-time (dbz#1713).

Rather than relying on the hard-to-tune combination of log.mining.batch.size.*, log.mining.sleep.time.*, and log.mining.scn.gap.detection.* properties, the connector now selects mining windows based on log file size and count, providing a more consistent and predictable workload regardless of SCN density. For the hybrid and online_catalog mining strategies, a new log.mining.log.count.min setting controls the minimum number of logs per redo thread to include in each mining session, while the redo_log_catalog strategy continues to read all available logs with a fixed one-second poll interval due to its data dictionary flushing requirements.

Users upgrading to this release should review their Oracle connector configurations and remove the now-obsolete batch-size, sleep-time, and SCN-gap-detection properties as part of the migration.

Improve logging for transaction log metadata

The Oracle connector’s LogMiner implementation now captures additional metadata for each log file, including its size on disk and the data dictionary start/end markers used by the redo_log_catalog strategy (dbz#1763). This information is surfaced in the LogFileCollector log output alongside the SCN delta range between the first and next boundaries for archive logs, giving users much clearer visibility into which logs are being collected and their characteristics during mining.

In addition, when redo log files are detected as inconsistent, the connector now logs a concise INFO-level message without the full stack trace; the previous behavior including the DebeziumException details remains available by enabling DEBUG logging. Together these changes make troubleshooting log collection issues significantly easier, especially in environments where the full log files are not readily available for inspection.

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Improved replication slot warning

The PostgreSQL connector now includes full exception details when it logs the warning about being unable to load replication slot information (dbz#1790). Previously, users saw only a generic message stating that Debezium would attempt to create the slot, with no indication of the underlying cause, forcing them to attach a debugger to diagnose issues such as transient network failures. With the SQLException now attached to the log entry, the stack trace is immediately visible, making it significantly easier to troubleshoot replication slot initialization problems in production environments.

Debezium JDBC sink

Agroal connection pool replaces C3P0

The JDBC sink connector now uses Agroal as its connection pool provider, replacing the previously bundled C3P0 pool shipped with Hibernate (dbz#1042). C3P0 had been a recurring source of connection management issues, and Agroal offers a more modern, reliable, and better-maintained pooling implementation. Users of the JDBC sink should benefit from improved stability and connection handling without any configuration changes required.

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Declaring tombstone support for batch processing

The Debezium Quarkus Extension’s @Capturing annotation for batch events now supports adding the supportsTombstoneEvents attribute, bringing batch consumers to feature parity with single-event capturing declarations (dbz#1751).

This allows sink implementations that process events in batches to declaratively indicate whether they can handle tombstone (null-value) records, enabling the runtime to correctly filter or forward deletion markers based on the consumer’s capabilities. The addition is a foundational piece of the broader effort to migrate Debezium Server from the legacy embedded engine API to the new debezium-quarkus-engine extension API, modernizing how sinks are wired into the Quarkus-based runtime.

Batch processing supports event headers

The BatchEvent class in the Debezium Quarkus Extension now exposes record headers alongside key and value data, giving batch-mode consumers access to the full metadata available on individual change events (dbz#1758).

This addition brings batch handling to parity with single-event processing and is a prerequisite for migrating Debezium Server sinks from the legacy embedded engine API to the new debezium-quarkus-engine extension API. Sink implementations that rely on headers for routing, filtering, or downstream propagation can now operate correctly when consuming events in batches.

Debezium Operator

Helm improvements and customizations

The Debezium Operator Helm chart has been reworked to allow much broader customization of deployment values (dbz#1212). Previously, the chart was generated by the Quarkus Operator SDK and exposed only a limited set of overridable options, which made it difficult to adapt to site-specific requirements.

Users can now override Kubernetes metadata, container images, and other configuration parameters directly through Helm values, making it significantly easier to integrate the Operator into diverse environments and GitOps workflows.

Debezium Platform

Improved data models for API resources

The Debezium Platform REST API now uses dedicated request and response data transfer objects (DTOs), implemented as Java records, instead of exposing Blazebit Entity Views directly on its endpoints. The previous approach was incompatible with the Bean Validation API, which degraded the user experience when submitting invalid payloads (dbz#1076).

Mapping between the new DTOs and the underlying entity views is handled by MapStruct, keeping service and persistence layers untouched while cleanly separating the external API model from internal representations. The JSON contract of the affected resources (Source, Destination, Transform, Vault, Connection, and Pipeline) is preserved, so existing API clients require no changes.

Updated source creation form

The Debezium Platform’s Pipeline designer has received an improved source creation experience (dbz#1808). Instead of relying on free-text input, the source creation form is now dynamically generated from the well-defined schemas, ensuring that users are presented with accurate, connector-specific configuration fields. This reduces configuration errors and makes it easier to discover and set the correct properties when building pipelines through the user interface.

Image pull policy support

The Helm chart now exposes imagePullPolicy as a configurable value for both the stage and conductor deployments, defaulting to IfNotPresent (dbz#1823). Previously, operators had to fork or patch the chart directly to override pull behavior, which was especially inconvenient in environments using custom image registries or frequently updated development tags. With this addition, users can tailor image pull policies to match their deployment workflows without modifying the chart itself.

New validators added

Several new connection validators were added, allowing users to verify connectivity directly from the platform user interface before configuring the sink pipelines.

  • Apache Pulsar (dbz#1083)

  • Google Pub/Sub (dbz#1092)

Debezium Server

New Amazon SNS sink

Debezium Server now includes a sink connector for Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS), expanding the set of AWS messaging targets available alongside the existing SQS and Kinesis sinks (dbz#739). The new sink uses the AWS SDK’s PublishBatch API to publish up to 10 messages per request, retries only the failed entries from a batch response, and forwards Debezium headers as SNS message attributes. It also supports FIFO topics with configurable headers for MessageGroupId and MessageDeduplicationId, as well as both single-topic and prefix-based multi-topic routing, giving users flexibility when fanning out change events to SNS subscribers. This enables event-driven architectures on AWS to consume CDC events directly from SNS without an intermediate broker.

HTTP sink OAuth2 authentication and batch support

The Debezium Server HTTP Client sink now supports OAuth2 client credentials grant authentication (RFC 6749 Section 4.4), complementing the existing JWT and Standard Webhooks options (dbz#1794). Users can configure the client ID, secret, token URL, scopes, client authentication method, HTTP method, and custom parameters to stream change events to OAuth2-protected HTTP endpoints.

In addition, a new batch mode has been introduced that aggregates multiple change events into a JSON array sent in a single HTTP POST request, controlled via the batch.enabled and batch.max-size options. This significantly reduces network overhead and improves throughput for high-volume CDC pipelines where per-event HTTP requests were previously a bottleneck.

Debezium for Cassandra

OpenTelemetry tracing support

The Cassandra connector now supports OpenTelemetry distributed tracing, bringing it in line with the observability capabilities available in other Debezium connectors (dbz#1769).

Because the Cassandra connector is not built on the Kafka Connect framework, the existing ActivateTracingSpan SMT cannot be used, so tracing has been instrumented directly at the Kafka Emitter level. For each emitted event, two nested spans are produced: a db-log-write span backdated to the original Cassandra mutation timestamp with source attributes such as keyspace, table, cluster, and commitlog position, and a debezium-read span capturing Debezium processing time along with the operation type. The trace context is propagated to downstream consumers through a traceparent header on the Kafka ProducerRecord, enabling end-to-end correlation across the pipeline.

The feature is opt-in and requires toggling the new tracing.enabled configuration property (disabled by default), and the connector will safely no-op if tracing is enabled without an OpenTelemetry JAR on the classpath.

Debezium for CockroachDB

Improved performance with cached event-specific schemas

The CockroachDB connector’s event-processing hot path has been optimized by eliminating a per-event allocation of CockroachDBPartition and its associated source-partition map, which previously occurred on every change event (dbz#1712). The partition is now initialized once and reused, matching how it is already handled for heartbeats.

Investigation also confirmed that the production path already benefits from cached TableSchema objects via RelationalDatabaseSchema, so the real overhead on top of raw JSON parsing is roughly 9% rather than the 3-4x gap originally suspected.

New JMH benchmarks covering the actual hot path (jsonParseAndColumnExtraction and columnExtractionOnly) have been added so future regressions can be measured against realistic workloads.

Debezium for Informix

Unsupported type improvements

The Informix connector now handles columns of unsupported types more gracefully by substituting their values with the configured unavailable.value.placeholder, rather than failing or producing incomplete events (dbz#1766). This applies to BYTE and TEXT columns, whose contents are not accessible through the Informix change streaming interface, and mirrors the approach already used for toasted values in the PostgreSQL connector.

With this change, users can capture changes from tables containing these column types without having to manually exclude them, making it easier to onboard existing Informix schemas for CDC.

Updated to JDBC driver v15

The Informix connector has been upgraded to use the Informix JDBC driver v15, which officially supports both Informix 14 and 15 and, in practice, continues to work with Informix 12 (dbz#1622). This upgrade enables the connector to leverage new capabilities introduced in Informix 15 that are only exposed by the newer driver, while still allowing users on older Informix releases to adopt the update before their version reaches end-of-life.

Container Images

The Debezium container images now detect the presence of a SCHEMA_REGISTRY environment variable on startup and automatically configure Avro serialization against the referenced registry (dbz#99).

When this variable is set, the entrypoint script enables the existing Apicurio converter integration and wires up the appropriate key and value Avro converters pointing at the given registry URL, removing the need to manually set ENABLE_APICURIO_CONVERTERS and the individual converter properties. This improvement simplifies getting started with schema-registry-backed deployments, particularly in tutorials and demo environments, while preserving the default behavior when no registry link is provided.

Debezium Examples

A new runnable Python example has been added that demonstrates how to consume Debezium change events directly in Connect mode (EngineFormat.CONNECT), bypassing the usual JSON serialization and deserialization step (dbz#1691). The example shows how to receive raw SourceRecord objects in Python, convert them into native dictionaries, and work with validated CDC event models.

This provides a useful starting point for developers integrating Debezium into Python-based data pipelines, AI systems, or frameworks such as LangChain and LangGraph, where avoiding JSON overhead and retaining richer event structure is beneficial.

entry.title: Overcoming Oracle CDC Replication Lag Through Collaboration

link.title: Overcoming Oracle CDC Replication Lag Through Collaboration

entry.content:
Introduction

At Pepkor NexTech, we have been using Debezium (with LogMiner) in our Oracle environments for around 4 years, and we currently maintain 12 Oracle instances.

Ingesting from Oracle with LogMiner creates unique challenges, with trade-offs that differ from other synchronous approaches (like trigger-based replication). We want to share how we resolved the resulting bottlenecks and alleviated persistent lag in our largest environment - an ERP system for a major retailer - by working directly with the source database team and DBAs.

The Problem

During the day, we kept up with the database’s churn. However, in the evenings, our Grafana lag metric (LagFromSourceInMilliseconds) would spike. On closer inspection, the duration of LogMiner fetch queries during this window increased significantly, sometimes taking over an hour before returning records.

We worked with the maintainers to improve the performance, adjusting Debezium parameters like batch size and query fetch size. Unfortunately, these tweaks didn’t yield the necessary gains, and over time, query fetch times had increased to such an extent that we were failing to catch up before the next evening’s batch load. It became clear that we were hitting the limits of what a purely configuration-based approach could solve with LogMiner.

Diagnosing the Root Cause - Log Analysis with LogMiner

To isolate which tables were responsible for the change volume, we executed ad hoc LogMiner queries to help us better understand the cause of the churn. First, we retrieved the archive logs for the window where our replication lag was spiking.

-- Identify archived logs generated between 7 PM and 9 PM
SELECT
    name,
    first_time,
    next_time
FROM
    v$archived_log
WHERE
    first_time >= TO_DATE('2026-03-01 19:00:00', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')
    AND next_time <= TO_DATE('2026-03-01 21:00:00', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')
    AND name IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY
    first_time;

For each log file, we would start a logminer session and then do a count of the number of changes in each file grouped by table_name and seg_owner. This query is typically performant as it excludes the sql_redo column.

BEGIN
  DBMS_LOGMNR.ADD_LOGFILE(
    '+FRA/PROD_DB/ARCHIVELOG/2026_03_01/thread_1_seq_99999',
    DBMS_LOGMNR.NEW
  );
  DBMS_LOGMNR.START_LOGMNR(
    OPTIONS  => DBMS_LOGMNR.DICT_FROM_ONLINE_CATALOG
  );
END;

SELECT
    TABLE_NAME,
    SEG_OWNER,
    COUNT(TABLE_NAME) AS TOTAL_COUNT
FROM
    V$LOGMNR_CONTENTS
WHERE
    TABLE_NAME IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY
    TABLE_NAME, SEG_OWNER
ORDER BY
    TOTAL_COUNT DESC;

Findings

The query results immediately identified the primary contributors to the redo log volume:

The top two tables — TEMP_FORECAST_BRANCH_WEEKLY and FORECAST_BRANCH_WEEKLY — collectively accounted for approximately 476.8 million redo operations, representing the overwhelming majority of log volume within the analysis window. Zooming out, we discovered this represented a sizable percentage of the database’s overall daily churn. Even though these tables were not in our table.include.list, the sheer amount of logging generated required LogMiner to churn through hundreds of millions of events, drastically slowing down our fetch queries.

Root Cause Analysis

The Source Process

The activity was traced to a nightly data refresh job implemented as a Korn shell (.ksh) script. The script was originally designed to ingest flat files into the database and populate a set of materialized views for downstream consumption.

The Impact of Truncate-and-Load on LogMiner

The script was executing a sequence that efficiently dropped and recreated materialized view data. While this established approach worked well for batch-oriented architectures with trigger-based replication, it inadvertently created a heavy workload for our continuous LogMiner process, which had to sequentially read through and parse all the generated logs.

A full truncate followed by a reload causes every row inserted into the target table to be recorded as a distinct insert event in the redo log, irrespective of whether that row’s data actually changed. For a table containing 100 million rows where only 500 rows have genuinely changed, a truncate-and-load still generates 100 million inserts that the LogMiner utility needs to fetch.

Remediation

Collaborating With the Source Team

We reached out to the source development team to better understand the underlying business requirements of the nightly job.

They were highly receptive, and once we explained the impact on CDC performance, both teams quickly aligned on evolving the ingestion from a truncate-and-load approach to a targeted merge-based pattern.

Step 1 — DDL Restructuring

The materialized view was dropped and replaced with a standard permanent table. An Oracle External Table was created, pointed directly at the working directory where the flat files are deposited. This eliminates the intermediate staging load entirely, allowing the database engine to query the source files directly.

Step 2 — Merge-Based Ingestion

The shell script logic was replaced with a PL/SQL procedure leveraging a MERGE INTO statement. To handle cases where the source flat files contained multiple records for the same key, an analytic deduplication step was applied using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY …​ ORDER BY last_update_date DESC) prior to the merge.

With this approach, only rows that have genuinely been inserted or modified generate corresponding redo events. This reduced log volume to the true delta of changes rather than a full-table reconstruction.

Outcome

Following the deployment of the merge-based procedure, we saw an immediate and significant improvement in query times. By aligning the generated redo logs with the actual change rate of the underlying data, replication lag was improved and the database’s overall compute overhead was substantially reduced.

As you can see by overlaying the metrics, there was a drastic reduction of load. Even though there are still some more expensive query cases taking over 10 minutes in the new implementation (peaking at ~12.3 minutes), the maximum duration plummeted from 95 minutes (5,700,000 ms). Furthermore, the average query time during the evening load window (from 7pm onwards) settled around 2.26 minutes (135,615 ms), completely avoiding the massive multi-hour replication lag previously experienced as LogMiner struggled to catch up.

This experience reinforces something often repeated by both the community and the maintainers of Debezium: Logminer performance is directly coupled to the behaviour of the source database, meaning design choices made upstream have real consequences for CDC throughput downstream.

When replication lag persists despite configuration tuning, the next step may be to have a conversation with the source team. The most resilient Oracle CDC environments tend to be those where data engineers and DBAs treat data loading patterns as a shared concern rather than problems that sit on either side of a boundary.
